content:
Hi all,

Is the use of (local) macros tolerated in code that might eventually be incorporated into Mathlib, or is it strictly forbidden?

The rationale is the following.

Lean has a bewilderingly large number of commands, not all of which are intuitively understandable—for example, have.

I am currently trying to formalise the differential form of Gronwall's
lemma, and I have found the following two macros useful (I have also
tested the code with the macros).

local macro "assume " xs:(ppSpace colGt term:max)+ : tactic =>
  `(tactic| intro $xs*)

local macro "claim " d:letDecl : tactic =>
  `(tactic| have $d:letDecl)

regards

Uwe Brauer

It is a bad idea to overwrite basic tactics like intro or have in mathlib, because people reading mathlib know these tactics very well, and would be confused to see a different tactic in their place. Overriding such basic tactics can be done for teaching purposes though.

Understood.

(I cannot, however, resist asking why intro should be considered more intuitive than assume, and have more intuitive than claim)

I searched the documentation: assume was available in Lean 3 and was valid syntax. Why was it changed?

In the development of GNU Emacs, to which I occasionally contribute, names are sometimes changed as well, but aliases are then introduced to preserve backward compatibility. Why is this not the case with Lean? (I did not really use Lean 3, so this is purely a matter of curiosity.)

The philosophy with tactics seems to be "don't have more than one way to do something". The computer scientists do not even like "lemma" in Lean, because it is the same as "theorem"; indeed "lemma" is not in core Lean, we have to add it in mathlib. Having synonymous tactics would be more confusing for AI and more confusing for students. You are saying "why don't we have X which does the same as Y". Let me turn the tables -- how do you answer a student who says "what is the point of X, if it just does exactly the same as Y?"
To add an example to Kevin's case: I have asker myself the latter question about lemmas and theorems because they seem to be to be used inconsistenly.

"Zn" == Zulip notifications <noreply@zulip.com> writes:

First of all, I would like to stress that I have not contributed a single line of Lean code to the project (although I hope that will change soon), so I am certainly not in a position to make demands.

I am also partly describing my own experience (and that of some colleagues) with Lean, and, for example, how I initially found intro somewhat difficult to understand.

Kevin Buzzard:

The philosophy with tactics seems to be "don't have more than one
way to do something". The computer scientists do not even like "lemma"
in Lean, because it is the same as "theorem"; indeed "lemma" is not in
core Lean, we have to add it in mathlib.

One thing I also miss is corollary. When reading the manuals, I had to remind myself that, in logic, a proposition does not quite mean the same thing as it does in the mathematical literature.

Having synonymous tactics
would be more confusing for AI and more confusing for students. You
are saying "why don't we have X which does the same as Y". Let me turn
the tables -- how do you answer a student who says "what is the point
of X, if it just does exactly the same as Y?"

I can also imagine students wondering, for example: intro — isn't that essentially the same as writing assume?

And, perhaps more generally, I wonder whether the choice of names such as have is necessarily intuitive to someone encountering Lean for the first time.

I think the issue you are fighting against is that these words which you don't like have become absolutely standard in the theorem prover community and have existed for decades across multiple systems, so there is broad consistency across communities which goes back a very long time. How would you react if a computer scientist knocked on your door and told you that they didn't like the way you were using some standard mathematical definition like "manifold" in your papers and said that it would be better if you renamed it to "shape" because they conjectured that it would make it easier to understand? That is how your request probably looks to the theorem prover community.

Theorem proving community does not have a problem with assume: after all, that's exactly what Isar uses. But Lean already has a notation, and adding an another one wins you nothing (you still need to know old notation and how things work) but adds confusion (the zoo of syntaxes got larger).

Uwe Brauer said:

local macro "assume " xs:(ppSpace colGt term:max)+ : tactic =>
  `(tactic| intro $xs*)

I forgot to mention, that this definition of assume is confusing: one usually assumes propositions, but xs here denotes hypothetical evidences of assumed propositions.

"Zn" == Zulip notifications <noreply@zulip.com> writes:

suhr:

@*Uwe Brauer|429732
<https://leanprover.zulipchat.com/#narrow/channel/287929-mathlib4/topic/the.20use.20of.20local.20macros.3A.20tolerated.3F.20forbidden.3F/near/629302134>:

local macro "assume " xs:(ppSpace colGt term:max)+ : tactic => (tactic| intro $xs*)

I forgot to mention, that this definition of assume is confusing:
one usually assumes propositions, but xs here denotes
hypothetical evidences of assumed propositions.

Thanks, that was helpful. When I first started working with proof assistants this summer, I began with Isabelle, as I found it much easier to read.
So I wrote code using assume or assumes, if I remember correctly. In Lean, it seemed to me that intro played the same role. I now realise that this is not quite true: intro is more general.
So I really ought to read the documentation more carefully before drawing conclusions, and, in particular, leave the standard commands alone.

Note, that we have a tactic called assume in mathlib. It is like intro but let's you specify the type instead of the name of the introduced variable:

import Mathlib.Tactic.Assume

open Function
example {α β γ} {g : β → γ} {f : α → β} (hg : Injective g) (hf : Injective f) :
    Injective (g ∘ f) := by
  intro x y
  -- same as `intro (_ : g (f x) = g (f y))`
  assume g (f x) = g (f y)
  have : f x = f y := by grind
  show x = y
  grind

It was considered to be a useful tactic for teaching but maybe not for usage inside mathlib, mostly because of the "don't have multiple options to do the same thing" spirit which Kevin mentioned. See Zulip topic.

If it's unclear, perhaps it should be mentioned that intro can be used for both ∀ x, ..., and P → ..., because of type theory. Obviously assume only makes sense for the latter.

On the topic of "don't have multiple ways to do the same thing", why do we have all of let, have and obtain?
... and as a rule of thumb, you should use let for types ("data", e.g. defining a map) and have for propositions.

arguably, rcases and obtain are exactly the same tactic, just a different user syntax. But deciding to prefer one is such a non-issue so there is no movement there. I believe historically intro, rintro and obtain were quite different in what they allowed (rcases-patterns) and meanwhile they've became more aligned. If they were added today, probably we wouldn't need all of them...

indeed, have forgets the term while let remembers it, so after have x := 2 you can't prove x=2 anymore because you only know x : Nat
